deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page reduces observations by Bessel, Gauss and others from autumn 1814 and tabulates their residuals. This page uses a set of elliptic elements to predict the next opposition. The elements fit (2) Pallas: node ≈172.6°, i ≈34.6°, e = sin φ ≈ 0.241, a ≈ 2.77, n ≈ 768.6"/day. The page gives the time of opposition, the geocentric position, the distance and the brightness.

Top (calendar arithmetic): 365·7 + 2 = 2557. Days are counted from 1810 Jan 0. 1810–1815 make 2191 days, and 1816 Jan 0 + 100 = 1816 April 9, giving day 2291. 2557 + 2291 = 4848 is the same date counted from 1803 Jan 0. Heading: 'Nächste Opposition ungefähr 1816 April 9 = 2291'.

Top right: log 2291 = 3.36007 and 9.13725 = log 0.13717"/day, i.e. about 50.1"/yr of precession. Their product is 314.25" = 5'14", the precession over 2291 days (interpretation mine).

Elements: ☊ = 172°35'6", i = 34°35'18", ϖ = 121°10'17", φ = 13°58'8" (e = sin φ), log a = 0.4429145, n = 768.62114"/day. Epoch day 1759 (= 1814 Oct 25) with mean longitude L0 = 64°5'18".

Step 1. Mean motion over Δt = 2291 − 1759 = 532 d:
- n·532 = 384310.57 + 23058.63 + 1537.24 = 408906.44".
- This is 113°35'6" mod 360°.
- L = 64°5'18" + 113°35'6" = 177°40'24".
- Mean anomaly M = L − ϖ = 56°30'7".

Step 2. Kepler's equation E − e″ sin E = M, with e″ = e·206265" (log e″ = 4.69717, e″ ≈ 49793").
- log sin E = 9.97146 gives e″ sin E = 12°57'6".
- Hence E = 69°27'13".
- The second-column logs (0.01922, 9.99068, 9.08491, …) seem to belong to the iteration and to v − E; I cannot certainly identify each one.

Step 3. Radius vector: log r = log a − log[1/(1 − e cos E)].
- Logs used: 0.61727 = log(1/e), 9.54527 = log cos E, 0.03844 obtained by Gaussian subtraction logarithm.
- log r = 0.44291 − 0.03844 = 0.40447, so r ≈ 2.538.

Step 4. True anomaly: v − E = 13°40'13", so v = 83°7'26" (equivalent to tan(v/2) = tan(45°+φ/2) tan(E/2)).

Step 5. Orbital longitude and argument of latitude:
- Orbital longitude v + ϖ = 204°17'43".
- u = 204°17'43" − ☊ = 31°42'37".
- tan(l − ☊) = cos i · tan u, using log tan u = 9.79089 and log cos i = 9.91553. The sum 9.70642 is not written. It gives l − ☊ = 26°57'37".
- Heliocentric longitude l = 199°32'43".
- tan β = tan i · sin(l − ☊): 9.83857 + 9.65645 = 9.49502, so heliocentric latitude β = 17°21'43".

Step 6. Time of opposition:
- The Sun's longitude is 19°29'8"; the Earth's heliocentric longitude 199°29'8" is written as ☉ 199°29'8".
- Difference: 3'35" = 215".
- Planet's daily heliocentric motion in longitude: dl/dt = n a² cos φ cos i /(r cos β)².
  - log(n a² cos φ cos i) = 3.67395.
  - 2 log(r cos β) = 2·0.38422 = 0.76844, with log cos β = 9.97975.
  - Result: 804.48"/day.
- Earth's daily motion: 3526".
- Relative motion: 2722" per day ('p.j.').
- Time: 215/2722 = 0.07899 d (logs 2.33244 − 3.43489 = 8.89755). Opposition on April 9.07899.
- Longitude at opposition: 199°33'47".

Step 7. Geocentric latitude at opposition (longitudes coincide):
- tan β' = r cos β tan β /(r cos β − R).
- log R = 0.00170; log(r cos β − R) = 0.15178.
- 0.38422 − 0.15178 = 0.23244; + 9.49502 = 9.72746.
- β' = 28°5'52".

Step 8. Distance and brightness:
- log Δ = 0.15178 − log cos β' (9.94554) = 0.20624.
- log(rΔ) = 0.20624 + 0.40447 = 0.61071; doubled = 1.22142.
- Brightness ('Licht') 1/(r²Δ²) = 10^−1.22142 = 0.06006.

Purpose: an approximate ephemeris for the coming Pallas opposition of 1816, to help astronomers find the planet. It is part of Gauss's routine minor-planet work c. 1814–15.
errors: No substantive errors found. The 532-day motion, mean anomaly, Kepler solution, argument of latitude, heliocentric latitude, opposition time, geocentric latitude, distance and brightness all recompute consistently to within the 5-place-log precision used.
log tan(26°57'37") recomputes to ≈9.70628 versus the implied 9.70642, and log tan β to ≈9.49494 versus the written 9.49502. These are last-digit rounding differences.
The coefficient 3.67395 recomputes as log(n a² cos φ cos i) ≈ 3.6740. The ~1e-4 difference is negligible.
The '9.20624 ld.' in the machine transcription must be 0.20624 = log Δ, as the following sum 0.20624 + 0.40447 = 0.61071 shows.

results.what: Opposition prediction for (2) Pallas: mean anomaly, Kepler equation, true anomaly, reduction to ecliptic, time of opposition from relative heliocentric motions, geocentric latitude, distance, and brightness 1/(r²Δ²)
results.modern_name: Two-body ephemeris computation / opposition prediction from osculating elements
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th–19th c. astronomical practice (Kepler, Euler, Lagrange; Gauss's Theoria Motus 1809 for the minor-planet setting)

results.what: Daily heliocentric motion in longitude = n a² cos φ cos i /(r cos β)² (areal-velocity law projected onto the ecliptic)
results.modern_name: Conservation of angular momentum (z-component), Kepler's second law

results.usually_credited_to: Hipparchus; numerical value from Bradley/Maskelyne/Bessel era

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine ephemeris calculation for Pallas of the kind Gauss performed and published regularly (e.g. in Monatliche Correspondenz and Zeitschrift für Astronomie). It contains no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: E = 69°27'13" solves Kepler's equation (≈0 to arcsecond level)

transcription_corrections: '9.20624 ld.' should read '0.20624 Δ' (log of geocentric distance).
The epoch reads 'Epoche Long. m. 1759^d', i.e. mean longitude at day 1759 counted from 1810 Jan 0 (= 1814 Oct 25).
'90552' in the right column is uncertain; it may be a log entry related to 0.07899 (log 0.07899 = 8.8976). The reading is doubtful.
The column entries 3.67395 / 0.76844 / 804"48 / 3526 / 2722" p.j. are the planet's daily heliocentric motion, the Earth's daily motion and their difference per day ('per jour').
